lessons.title: Study Session 1: Building an Editorial Calendar Across Content Types and Contributors

blocks.text: Introduction Ndalu Cassinda coordinates content for a regional agricultural extension programme in Lubango, where a newsletter writer, a radio scriptwriter and a flyer designer each scheduled their own work independently, producing weeks where all three released material on the same topic within days of each other, followed by weeks where nothing from the programme appeared at all. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about structured content planning practice among marketers. Distinguish an editorial calendar spanning multiple content types and contributors from a single-channel posting schedule. Apply a method for building a calendar that coordinates several contributors and formats at once. Recognise when a calendar has become too rigid or too loose to actually guide the team. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Five Pieces One Week, Then Nothing the Next Ndalu Cassinda coordinates content for a regional agricultural extension programme based in Lubango, where a newsletter writer, a radio scriptwriter and a flyer designer each planned their own schedule independently. A review of the programme's output across two months found one week where all three had, by coincidence, covered the same seasonal planting advice within days of each other, followed by nearly three weeks where the programme published nothing at all. 2.2 What Research Found About Structured Content Planning In 2014, the researchers Geoff Holliman and Jennifer Rowley published a study in the Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing examining how business-to-business marketers actually approached digital content marketing. Their finding was that structured content planning practice, including a shared editorial calendar coordinating what would be produced, by whom, and when, distinguished more mature, effective content operations from those still producing content on an ad hoc basis, where individual contributors each made their own scheduling decisions without reference to what anyone else was doing. 2.3 Coordinating a Calendar Across Formats and People Putting Every Contributor and Format on One Shared Calendar Placing every contributor's planned content, regardless of format, newsletter, radio script, flyer, on one shared calendar rather than several separate personal ones, is what actually lets overlaps and gaps become visible before they happen rather than after. Spacing Topics Deliberately Rather Than by Coincidence Reviewing the shared calendar for topic overlap and coverage gaps before a period begins, rather than discovering them once content has already gone out, lets a team space related topics deliberately instead of leaving the spacing to chance. 2.4 Key Practices Place every contributor's planned content, across every format, on one shared calendar. Review the shared calendar for topic overlap and coverage gaps before a planning period begins. Space related topics deliberately rather than leaving their timing to individual coincidence. Revisit the calendar's structure when it starts to feel too rigid to adjust or too loose to actually guide anyone. 2.5 A Worked Example: Ndalu's Shared Calendar Ndalu built a single shared calendar visible to the newsletter writer, the radio scriptwriter and the flyer designer, listing each planned piece, its format, its contributor and its intended release week, and set a short review at the start of each month where the three compared what was planned before finalising it. Over the following quarter, the programme's output spread more evenly across the weeks, and a planned overlap on a fertiliser topic was caught during the monthly review and staggered two weeks apart instead. Each contributor had continued producing genuinely useful material the whole time. What the programme had been missing was simply one place where all three plans could actually be seen together before anything went out. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Letting each contributor maintain a separate personal schedule, with no shared view of what the whole team is producing, allows genuine overlaps and gaps to form without anyone noticing until content has already been published or a week has already gone quiet. A calendar built once and never revisited can become either too rigid to accommodate a genuine change or too loose to actually guide anyone's planning. 2.7 Coincidence Is a Poor Substitute for a Shared View Every piece the extension programme's three contributors had produced separately was genuinely useful on its own. Bringing their plans onto one shared calendar did not change what any of them were capable of producing. It simply gave the three of them, for the first time, a way to see each other's plans before the week the content actually went out. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to build a shared editorial calendar coordinating multiple contributors and content types at once. Study Session 2 turns from the shared calendar to the individual briefs that tell each contributor exactly what they own within it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a team or organisation producing more than one type of content. Does everyone involved have a shared view of what everyone else is planning? 2. Sketch a one-month shared calendar for one real content operation, naming at least two contributors and two different content formats. Practical Output: Practical Output A one-month shared editorial calendar for one real content operation, listing at least two contributors, their formats, and a scheduled monthly review point. 7.0 References and Further Reading Holliman, G., & Rowley, J. (2014). Business to business digital content marketing: Marketers' perceptions of best practice. Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing, 8(4), 269 to 293. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 20:18, on plans being established through counsel, and war being waged with wise guidance. Qur'an, Surah Al-Furqan 25:2, on Him who has created each thing and determined it with precise determination.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Assigning Content Briefs With Clear Ownership and Deadlines

blocks.text: Introduction Boureima Zongo manages a small team of freelance writers producing a trade association's newsletter from Bobo-Dioulasso, and after asking two different writers to each write something about the coming harvest season without specifying who owned the topic or when it was due, discovered a week before publication that neither had actually written it, each having assumed the other was handling it. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what goal-setting research found about clarity and task motivation. Distinguish a content brief with clear ownership and a deadline from a vague, open-ended assignment. Apply a method for writing a brief specific enough for a contributor to act on without further clarification. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Nobody Was Sure Who Owned It Boureima Zongo manages a small team of freelance writers producing a trade association's newsletter from Bobo-Dioulasso, and had asked two different writers, in separate casual conversations, to each write something about the coming harvest season, without specifying which of them actually owned the topic or by when it was needed. A week before the newsletter's publication date, Boureima discovered neither writer had produced anything, each having assumed the other was handling it. 2.2 What Research Found About Goal Clarity and Task Motivation In 2002, the researchers Edwin Locke and Gary Latham published a study in American Psychologist summarising thirty-five years of research on goal setting and task motivation. Their central finding was that specific, clear goals consistently produced higher performance than vague or general ones, and that ambiguity about exactly what a task required, and who was responsible for it, reliably undermined the motivation and follow-through needed to actually complete it. 2.3 Writing a Brief a Contributor Can Act On Naming One Owner for Every Assigned Topic Assigning a topic to exactly one named contributor, rather than mentioning it to more than one person or leaving it unassigned, removes the ambiguity that let Boureima's harvest season article go unwritten by two people who each assumed the other had it. Making a Deadline and Scope Specific Enough to Act On Writing a brief that states a specific deadline, a specific angle, and a specific length or format, rather than a general topic alone, gives a contributor everything needed to begin work without a further round of clarifying questions. 2.4 Key Practices Assign a topic to exactly one named contributor, never to more than one person at once. State a specific deadline in every brief, rather than leaving timing open or implied. Name a specific angle and format in the brief, not only a general subject area. Confirm the contributor has actually seen and accepted the brief, not only that it was sent. Check in partway through a longer deadline rather than only at the due date. 2.5 A Worked Example: Boureima's Written Briefs Boureima began sending every assignment as a short written brief naming one owner, a specific deadline, a specific angle, and a target length, and asked each writer to reply confirming they had seen it. For the next harvest season feature, he assigned it to one writer alone, with a brief specifying a farmer-interview angle and a deadline ten days ahead of publication. The article arrived four days early, and no assignment was ever again mistakenly left to two writers' shared assumption. Both writers from the earlier confusion had been genuinely willing to write the piece. What had actually been missing was a brief specific enough that either of them could have started without first checking whether the other had already begun. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Mentioning a topic to more than one contributor, even informally, without naming a single clear owner, leaves each person reasonably able to assume someone else is handling it. A brief that names only a general subject, without a specific deadline, angle or format, forces a contributor to guess at details that should have been settled before work began. 2.7 Willingness Alone Never Produced the Article Neither writer had lacked the willingness or the skill to produce the harvest season piece. What stood between two capable writers and a finished article was nothing more than a missing name attached clearly enough to the assignment that one of them could act on it without hesitation. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to write a content brief with clear ownership and a specific deadline. Study Session 3 turns from assigning content clearly to reviewing it properly before it ever reaches an audience.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a task you were once assigned informally, without a clear deadline or sole owner. What happened as a result? 2. Write a short content brief for one real topic, naming a single owner, a specific deadline, an angle and a format. Practical Output: Practical Output A written content brief for one real assignment, naming a single owner, a specific deadline, a specific angle, and a target format or length. 7.0 References and Further Reading Locke, E.A., & Latham, G.P. (2002). Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey. American Psychologist, 57(9), 705 to 717. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Romans 14:12, on each of us giving an account of ourselves. Qur'an, Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:1, on fulfilling contracts and obligations.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Running a Review and Approval Workflow Before Publishing

blocks.text: Introduction Senait Habte, who has managed on her own since being widowed some years ago, coordinates content for a microfinance cooperative in Keren, and let contributors publish directly to the cooperative's channels until a piece containing an inaccurate interest rate figure reached the full membership list before anyone caught the error. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what gatekeeping research established about the selection process before publication. Distinguish a defined review and approval workflow from publishing whatever a contributor submits directly. Apply a method for building a simple review step before content goes live. Identify when a review step has become a bottleneck rather than a safeguard. Recognise when content has bypassed the review process entirely. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 An Inaccurate Number Reached Every Member Senait Habte coordinates content for a microfinance cooperative based in Keren, and until recently, any contributor could publish directly to the cooperative's channels without anyone else reviewing the piece first. A newsletter article citing an outdated interest rate figure went out to the cooperative's entire membership list, and the error was only caught after several members had already called in confused about which figure was actually correct. 2.2 What Gatekeeping Research Established In 1950, the researcher David Manning White published a study in Journalism Quarterly examining how a wire editor at a small newspaper decided which news items to publish and which to discard, establishing what became known as gatekeeping theory. White's central finding was that a designated reviewer's judgment functioned as a genuine gate, shaping what content actually reached an audience, and that this review step was not a formality but a substantive check capable of catching an error or a poor decision before it became public. 2.3 Building a Review Step That Actually Works Naming a Specific Reviewer Before Content Goes Live Assigning a specific person to review a piece of content before it publishes, rather than leaving publication open to whichever contributor finishes first, restores the substantive check that Senait's cooperative had gone without. Keeping the Review Step Fast Enough to Actually Be Used Setting a realistic turnaround time for a review, and reviewing content in the order it is submitted, keeps the step quick enough that contributors do not start bypassing it simply to avoid a delay. 2.4 Key Practices Assign a specific named reviewer for content before it is allowed to publish. Set a realistic turnaround time for review so the step does not become a bottleneck. Check factual claims, figures and dates specifically during review, not only tone and grammar. Track whether any content has published without going through the review step, and address it directly. 2.5 A Worked Example: Senait's Review Step Senait introduced a simple rule that no piece could publish to the cooperative's channels without her review or that of one other designated reviewer, with a standard one-day turnaround, and added a specific check for figures and dates to the review checklist given the earlier interest rate error. In the following months, two further draft errors, an outdated branch address and a misstated repayment deadline, were caught during review before publication, neither reaching a single member. The contributors who had written the flawed pieces were experienced and generally careful. What had been missing was not their competence but a second set of eyes positioned to catch what any one contributor, working alone, was always going to occasionally miss. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Allowing any contributor to publish directly without a review step removes the substantive check that catches a factual error before it reaches an audience, which is precisely the gap that let the cooperative's interest rate figure through. A review step that takes too long, however, risks contributors quietly bypassing it under deadline pressure, which defeats its purpose just as thoroughly as never having one at all. 2.7 A Careful Writer Still Needs a Second Reader The contributor who published the incorrect interest rate figure was neither careless nor inexperienced. Every writer occasionally lets an error slip past their own read of their own work, and it took a second, dedicated reader to catch what the piece's own author had already looked at and missed. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to set up a review and approval step that catches an error before content reaches an audience. Study Session 4 turns from catching errors before publication to keeping tone and formatting consistent across everything that does get published.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a piece of content you or your organisation published recently. Did it go through a review step before publishing, or straight from writer to audience? 2. Design a simple review checklist for one real content operation, naming a reviewer, a turnaround time, and one specific thing to check beyond tone and grammar. Practical Output: Practical Output A review workflow for one real content operation, naming a designated reviewer, a realistic turnaround time, and a checklist including a check for factual accuracy. 7.0 References and Further Reading White, D.M. (1950). The gatekeeper: A case study in the selection of news. Journalism Quarterly, 27, 383 to 391. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 1 John 4:1, on testing the spirits to see whether they are from God. Qur'an, Surah An-Nur 24:16, on not speaking of a matter without knowledge.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Ndalu's programme had one week with three pieces on the same topic and nearly three weeks with nothing published. What did this reveal?
options: The programme's contributors were not producing enough content overall
Separate personal schedules with no shared view can produce genuine overlaps and gaps without anyone noticing
Agricultural extension programmes should not use multiple content formats
Ndalu had failed to hire enough contributors
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Building an Editorial Calendar Across Content Types and Contributors) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Holliman and Rowley's 2014 research, what distinguished more mature content marketing operations?
options: Producing the largest possible volume of content
Structured content planning practice, including a shared editorial calendar
Relying exclusively on a single content format
Avoiding any collaboration between contributors
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Building an Editorial Calendar Across Content Types and Contributors) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend placing on one shared calendar?
options: Only content from the most senior contributor
Every contributor's planned content, across every format
Only content already published, for record-keeping purposes
Only content scheduled for the current week
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Building an Editorial Calendar Across Content Types and Contributors) before continuing.

quiz.q: Two writers each assumed the other was writing the harvest season article, and neither produced it. What did this reveal?
options: Both writers lacked the skill needed for the assignment
Mentioning a topic to more than one person without naming a single owner leaves ownership genuinely ambiguous
Trade association newsletters should not cover seasonal topics
Boureima had assigned too many topics overall
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Assigning Content Briefs With Clear Ownership and Deadlines) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Locke and Latham's 2002 research, what consistently produced higher performance?
options: Vague, general goals that allowed flexibility
Specific, clear goals, as opposed to vague or ambiguous ones
Goals set without any deadline attached
Goals assigned to multiple people simultaneously
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Assigning Content Briefs With Clear Ownership and Deadlines) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend including in every content brief?
options: Only a general subject area, left otherwise open
A single named owner, a specific deadline, and a specific angle and format
A list of every contributor who might be interested in the topic
No deadline, to allow maximum contributor flexibility
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Assigning Content Briefs With Clear Ownership and Deadlines) before continuing.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Maintaining a Style Guide for Consistent Tone and Formatting

blocks.text: Introduction Braima Djalo coordinates communications for a regional trade union in Gabu, where a style guide written two years earlier still technically existed on a shared drive, but nobody had opened it in months, and the union's recent publications showed dates written three different ways and a tone swinging from formal to casual within the same newsletter issue. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about corporate style guides and writing consistency. Distinguish a maintained, actively used style guide from one written once and then forgotten. Apply a method for checking a piece of content against a style guide before publishing. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Style Guide Nobody Opened Anymore Braima Djalo coordinates communications for a regional trade union based in Gabu, and a style guide written two years earlier still technically existed on the union's shared drive, though a review of recent output found nobody had referred to it in months. The union's last three newsletter issues showed dates written three different ways, headers formatted inconsistently, and a tone swinging from formal in one article to noticeably casual in the next. 2.2 What Research Found About Corporate Style Guides In 2005, the researcher Mark Bright published a study in Technical Communication examining how organisations create, implement and maintain corporate style guides. His finding was that a style guide's value depended entirely on active maintenance and genuine use, and that without deliberate upkeep and buy-in from contributors, team members reliably defaulted to their own individual preferences, producing exactly the kind of inconsistency, in formatting, tone and terminology, that a style guide was originally meant to prevent. 2.3 Keeping a Style Guide in Active Use Making the Style Guide Easy to Actually Check Against Keeping a style guide short, specific and easy to locate, rather than long and buried in a folder nobody remembers to open, is what actually determines whether contributors refer to it before writing rather than after a problem is pointed out. Checking New Content Against the Guide Before It Publishes Adding a specific check against the style guide as part of the review step, rather than treating the guide as background reference material, is what keeps a style guide's rules connected to what actually gets published. 2.4 Key Practices Keep the style guide short, specific and easy to locate, not long and buried in a folder. Check new content against the style guide as a specific part of the review step. Update the style guide itself when a genuine, recurring exception to it emerges. Revisit the style guide with contributors periodically, not only when it is first written. 2.5 A Worked Example: Braima's Revived Style Guide Braima trimmed the union's two-year-old style guide down to a single page covering date format, header style, and preferred tone, pinned it to the top of the shared drive folder contributors used daily, and added a specific line to the review checklist asking whether a submitted piece matched the guide's date format, headers and tone. The following newsletter issue showed a single consistent date format and header style throughout, and the tone, while still allowing some natural variation between writers, no longer swung sharply from one article to the next. The union's contributors had never been careless about consistency by choice. Consistency had simply stopped being anyone's specific responsibility to check, until the guide was made short enough to actually use and built directly into the review step. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Writing a style guide once and filing it away, without building any specific check against it into the ongoing review process, allows contributors to quietly drift back toward their own individual preferences, which is exactly what wore down the union's newsletter over two years. A style guide too long or too general to check against quickly tends to go unused for the same reason a missing guide does. 2.7 Existing Somewhere Is Not the Same as Being Used The union's original style guide had never been wrong in its content. Sitting unopened on a shared drive for months, however accurate its rules remained, had left it doing no more good than if it had never been written at all. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to keep a style guide in active use through a specific check built into the review step. Study Session 5 turns from keeping new content consistent to managing the growing backlog and archive of content already published.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a style guide, formal or informal, that your own team or organisation has. When was it last actually checked against a piece of content before publishing? 2. Draft a one-page style guide summary for one real content operation, covering date format, header style and preferred tone. Practical Output: Practical Output A one-page style guide for one real content operation, covering date format, header style and preferred tone, with a specific check built into the review process. 7.0 References and Further Reading Bright, M.R. (2005). Creating, implementing, and maintaining corporate style guides in an age of technology. Technical Communication, 52(1), 42 to 51. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Titus 1:5, on putting in order what was left unfinished. Qur'an, Surah An-Nahl 16:89, on the Book sent down as clarification for all things.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Managing a Content Backlog and Archive Over Its Full Lifecycle

blocks.text: Introduction Garmai Kollie, who cares for her young nephew most afternoons while managing content for a community health organisation in Gbarnga, discovered during an unrelated site review that a health guidance article published four years earlier, and since contradicted by updated national guidance, was still live on the organisation's website and still among its most-read pages. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about structured governance across a content or data asset's lifecycle. Distinguish an actively managed backlog and archive from content left to accumulate unmanaged. Apply a method for reviewing a backlog and retiring or archiving outdated content. Set a policy for how long content stays active before it is reviewed for archival. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 An Outdated Guidance Article Still Being Read Garmai Kollie manages content for a community health organisation based in Gbarnga, and during an unrelated review of the organisation's website, discovered a health guidance article published four years earlier, since contradicted by updated national guidance, that had never been revised or removed. The article remained live and, according to the site's own analytics, was still among the organisation's most-read pages. 2.2 What Research Found About Governance Across a Lifecycle In 2019, the researchers Rene Abraham, Johannes Schneider and Jan vom Brocke published a study in the International Journal of Information Management reviewing structured governance practices for information and data assets. Their finding was that whether an information asset remained valuable, accurate and genuinely accessible depended on deliberate governance across its entire lifecycle, not only at the point of creation, and that content left unmanaged after publication tended to accumulate unreviewed, with outdated material sitting indefinitely alongside current, accurate material with no way for a reader to distinguish between them. 2.3 Reviewing a Backlog Across Its Lifecycle Reviewing Older Content on a Set Schedule, Not by Accident Scheduling a periodic review of older published content specifically for continued accuracy, rather than relying on someone happening to notice a problem, is what would have caught Garmai's outdated guidance article years before an unrelated review finally surfaced it. Setting a Clear Policy for When Content Gets Archived Deciding in advance how long a piece of content remains presumed current before it is flagged for review, rather than leaving that decision to whenever someone happens to look, gives a backlog a genuine, predictable lifecycle rather than an indefinite one. 2.4 Key Practices Schedule a periodic review of older published content specifically for continued accuracy. Set a clear policy for how long content remains presumed current before review. Archive or clearly flag outdated content rather than leaving it live and unmarked. Prioritise reviewing content on topics most likely to change, such as guidance or figures. Record when a piece of content was last reviewed, not only when it was first published. 2.5 A Worked Example: Garmai's Lifecycle Review Garmai removed the outdated guidance article immediately and replaced it with current, verified content, then built a policy flagging any health guidance content for mandatory review after eighteen months, prioritising exactly the kind of material most likely to change. She also added a visible "last reviewed" date to every guidance page going forward. A full backlog review over the following month surfaced two further articles, both now updated, that had similarly outlived their accuracy without anyone noticing. The organisation's writers had never published anything they knew to be false at the time. Content simply has a lifespan the moment it touches guidance that can change, and nothing in the organisation's process had ever been built to notice when that lifespan quietly ran out. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Leaving published content unreviewed indefinitely, on the assumption that once-accurate material stays accurate forever, allows outdated guidance to sit alongside current material with no way for a reader to tell them apart, exactly as happened with Garmai's four-year-old article. Reviewing a backlog only when a problem happens to surface, rather than on a set schedule, leaves an organisation dependent on chance to catch what a policy could catch reliably instead. 2.7 A Backlog Left Alone Does Not Stay Neutral The health organisation's older content had not sat quietly and harmlessly for four years simply because nobody looked at it. Readers had kept finding and trusting an article the organisation itself no longer stood behind, the entire time no one was checking. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to manage a content backlog and archive across its full lifecycle, reviewing and retiring outdated material on a set schedule. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how the whole editorial operation is checked, periodically, against the original plan.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of older content your own organisation has published. When was it last reviewed for continued accuracy? 2. Set a review policy for one real content archive, naming how long content stays presumed current before it is flagged for review. Practical Output: Practical Output A content lifecycle review policy for one real archive, naming a review interval, a priority category of content, and a plan for flagging or archiving outdated material. 7.0 References and Further Reading Abraham, R., Schneider, J., & vom Brocke, J. (2019). Data governance: A conceptual framework, structured review, and research agenda. International Journal of Information Management, 49, 424 to 438. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Ecclesiastes 3:6, on a time to keep and a time to throw away. Qur'an, Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:77-78, on an honourable Qur'an in a well-protected Register.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Reviewing Editorial Output Periodically Against the Plan

blocks.text: Introduction Aristide Yangoua leads communications planning for a regional development NGO in Bambari, and had never once compared what the NGO's team actually published against the quarterly editorial calendar he built at the outset of each cycle, until a funder's routine question about the past quarter's output sent him back to check, and he found barely half of what had been planned had actually been produced. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle established about periodic review against a plan. Distinguish a scheduled review of editorial output from an ad hoc glance at what happened to get published. Apply a method for comparing actual editorial output against the original calendar and briefs. Set a recurring interval for the review going forward. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Half the Plan, and No One Had Noticed Aristide Yangoua leads communications planning for a regional development NGO based in Bambari, and built a fresh editorial calendar at the outset of every quarter, assuming, without ever actually checking, that most of what was planned generally got produced. A funder's routine question about the previous quarter's communications output sent him back through the records for the first time, and he found barely half of the quarter's planned pieces had actually been published, with no one on the team having flagged the gap along the way. 2.2 What the Plan-Do-Check-Act Cycle Established In his 1986 book Out of the Crisis, published by MIT Press, the statistician and management thinker W. Edwards Deming set out the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, a structured approach built on the principle that a plan is only useful if what actually happened is checked against it afterward, and any gap is then used to adjust the next cycle. Deming's argument was that skipping the check step, assuming a plan was followed simply because it existed, left an organisation with no real way to know whether its work was actually going as intended. 2.3 Checking Actual Output Against the Plan Comparing the Calendar to What Actually Published Setting the original calendar and the record of what actually published side by side, item by item, is what actually reveals a gap between plan and reality, rather than a general impression that things had probably gone well enough. Using the Gap to Adjust the Next Cycle, Not Just Note It Asking specifically why a planned piece was not produced, a brief that was never assigned, a deadline that slipped, a reviewer who became unavailable, turns a review from a simple tally into something that can actually change how the next quarter's calendar is built. 2.4 Key Practices Compare the original calendar to the record of what actually published, item by item. Ask specifically why each unproduced piece fell through, rather than simply recording that it did. Use what the review finds to adjust how the next planning cycle is built. Set a recurring interval for this review, rather than waiting for an outside question to prompt it. 2.5 A Worked Example: Aristide's Quarterly Check Aristide built a simple comparison sheet listing every item from the quarter's calendar alongside whether it had actually published, and for each gap, noted a specific reason, three pieces had never been assigned a named owner, two had lost their reviewer partway through with no replacement assigned. He used these findings to add a stricter ownership check to the next quarter's calendar process and set the comparison review itself as a recurring task at the end of every quarter. The following quarter's output matched the plan far more closely, and the specific gap in unassigned ownership did not recur. Nothing about the NGO's team had been unable to do the work the calendar called for. The plan itself had simply never been checked against reality closely enough to notice, quarter after quarter, exactly where it kept quietly falling short. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Assuming a plan was generally followed, without ever comparing it item by item against what actually published, allows a substantial gap to go unnoticed for a long stretch of time, which is how the NGO's quarterly output drifted as far as it did. Noting that a gap exists without asking specifically why each piece was missed wastes the review's real value, since the same gap is then likely to recur in the next cycle. 2.7 A Plan Unchecked Behaves Like No Plan at All Aristide's quarterly calendars had never been unrealistic or poorly built. Without ever being checked against what actually happened, though, a perfectly reasonable plan had been quietly drifting from reality for who knew how many quarters before a funder's question finally forced the comparison. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to compare actual editorial output against the original plan on a recurring schedule, using any gap to adjust the next cycle. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Copywriting and Message Craft, the next course in Pathway 48.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a plan or calendar your own work follows. Has anyone ever compared what actually happened against it, item by item? 2. Build a simple comparison sheet for one real editorial period, naming at least three planned items and whether each was actually completed. Practical Output: Practical Output A comparison review for one real editorial period, listing planned items against actual output, naming a specific reason for any gap, and a recurring interval for repeating the review. 7.0 References and Further Reading Deming, W.E. quiz.q: The union's style guide existed but had not been used in months, and recent output showed visible inconsistency. What did this reveal?
options: The style guide's original rules had been incorrect
A style guide's value depends on active maintenance and use, not merely existing somewhere
Trade unions should not maintain written style guides at all
The union's contributors lacked basic writing skill

quiz.q: According to Bright's 2005 research, what happens without deliberate style guide maintenance and buy-in?

Team members reliably default to their own individual preferences, producing inconsistency
Style guides become more effective over time without any upkeep
Consistency improves as a style guide ages
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Maintaining a Style Guide for Consistent Tone and Formatting) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend to keep a style guide in active use?
options: Making it as long and comprehensive as possible

Avoiding any written guide in favour of individual contributor judgment

quiz.q: An outdated health guidance article remained live and among the most-read pages four years after publication. What did this reveal?

Community health organisations should not publish guidance content
The article's analytics had been recorded incorrectly

quiz.q: According to Abraham, Schneider and vom Brocke's 2019 research, what did an information asset's continued value depend on?

Deliberate governance across its entire lifecycle, not only at creation

Whether it was the organisation's oldest published content
